newsitem.title: CHINA: POLL-HK growth seen robust despite property moves.
newsitem.headline: POLL-HK growth seen robust despite property moves.

text.p: Hong Kong's economy is expected to grow at a healthy clip into 1998, with any negative impact from measures taken by the post-handover government to cool the property market likely to be modest, analysts said.

"The property market will definitely have an impact on consumption, and this year the economy has been mainly driven by the domestic sector," said George Leung, economic adviser to Hongkong Bank. But the impact should be mild, he said.

Economists polled by Reuters on average expected the territory's gross domestic product (GDP) to increase by 5.64 percent in 1997 and 5.57 percent in 1998. Consumer prices were expected to rise 6.59 percent this year and 7.0 percent next year.
The forecasts compare with GDP growth of 4.7 percent for all of 1996, and inflation of 6.0 percent the same year.

Hongkong Bank said in a report issued on Thursday that while both investment and consumer spending were expected to expand strongly in the second half of the year, growth may be slower than in the first quarter due to a cooling off in the property market.

In its report, Hongkong Bank raised its forecast for 1997 GDP growth to 5.4 percent from 5.2 percent, based on a better-than-expected performance in the first quarter driven by strong domestic demand.
It trimmed its inflation forecast to 6.4 percent from 6.8 percent, owing to a sharp drop in food prices in the first half of the year.
Economists have estimated first quarter growth of about six percent. Government figures will be released on Monday.

"Spending is going to remain on an uptrend with moderating inflation and rising real income and that is going to offset the external drag from the trade deficit," said Chi Lo, regional economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell (Singapore).

In his first policy address following the July 1 handover, Hong Kong Chief Executive Tung Chee-hwa announced plans to boost housing supply as a way to moderate real estate price rises and make homes more affordable.
Hong Kong returned to Chinese rule on July 1 after more than 150 years of British colonial rule.
Economists said that as long as the government used supply-boosting rather than demand-crimping measures to deal with the housing problem, the effect on growth should be slight.
"We expect the government to pursue increasing supply as the main measure for curbing the market rather than using any tax measures," said DMG's Lo.
As a result, "the underlying trend for asset markets in Hong Kong which include the property and the stock markets, is still up, and that goes into our baseline assumption for GDP growth," he said.
Ken Chan, senior economist at Nikko Securities, said a modest decline in property values would be welcomed.

"If the decline is limited to 10-15 percent it is kind of healthy so you wouldn't expect a negative impact on next year's growth," he said. The economist said Nikko has forecast slightly lower growth in 1998 because of an expected decline in private consumption.
HSBC's Leung said that barring the adoption of any draconian measures to curb speculation, he expected property prices to rise again next year, though by a smaller magnitude than in 1997.
Property values had risen 30 percent during the first half of 1997.
Leung said his forecast of 5.3 to 5.7 percent growth next year assumed that the government will stick with a long-term policy of increasing housing supply.

"If we see a lot of drastic moves in October, then the forecast would be another story," he said. Chief Executive Tung will deliver an address to the legislature in October, when he is expected to elaborate on his housing goals.
The economists also said they expected the Hong Kong dollar to be little changed at end-1997, despite recent volatility in the wake of currency instability in the rest of Asia.
